item.description:
The big one. What started as a testing + cleanup pass grew into Pits’ largest release yet: accurate cost, a per-turn cost breakdown, a live “working vs. waiting on you” indicator, in-app Claude Code cache/retention controls, and a batch of reliability fixes — on top of the testing foundation the release was originally scoped around.

  • Costs are right now. The Claude 5 family (Fable, Mythos) was silently priced at $0 — a whole model family missing from the rate table — so recent usage undercounted badly. Fixed, and Sonnet 5 now bills at its $2/$10 introductory rate through 2026-08-31 to match real invoices. Rates are looked up live from the LiteLLM price feed daily, with the bundled table as a durable fallback.
  • Click a row to see what each turn cost. Every message you sent expands into a per-turn breakdown — its context charge and total, newest first — so you can tell which prompt was expensive and why, instead of staring at one opaque total.
  • See what a cache miss cost you. When a send lands on an expired cache, the context charge shows the warm price it would have paid, struck through, ahead of the cold price it actually paid — on the collapsed row, on each affected turn in the breakdown, and immediately while a send is still in flight.
  • Live “working vs. waiting on you.” The status dot is a spinning arc while Claude is working and a steady dot when the ball’s in your court. And a run that dies without a clean finish — spend-limit, an interrupt, a compaction, an API error — no longer leaves the row spinning forever; run-boundary markers settle it. (A 3½-hour phantom “working” state after a spend-limit hit is what prompted this.)
  • A Context Size column. Each conversation shows the model it’s on and how full its context window is (“Opus 4.8” over “461k”), in its own column paired with Context Charge — the size of the window, then what re-submitting it will cost next turn. In the expanded breakdown, every turn shows the tokens it submitted (the running context total, which climbs through a conversation and drops after a compaction), and the model name is printed on the turn where it changed, so a mid-conversation model switch is visible right where it happened.
  • “N turns” counts messages you actually sent. Slash commands, machine-injected wrappers, background-task notifications, and tool results no longer inflate the count — a turn is a message you typed.
  • Cache-expiry chimes only fire when a conversation is waiting on you. No more “your cache is about to expire” sound while Claude is mid-run and nobody’s waiting on the prompt.
  • Pits notices when it was killed. If macOS terminates Pits in the background (memory pressure while the Mac sleeps was the likely overnight culprit), the next launch says so instead of silently resuming — and Pits now shuts down cleanly on SIGTERM so a normal quit isn’t mistaken for a crash.
  • Follows the calendar on its own. Crossing midnight prepends a “Today” section and scrolls to it; crossing into a new month no longer needs a relaunch to start showing that month’s conversations.
  • Claude Code controls in the toolbar. Two menus — cache lifetime (Automatic / 5 minutes / 1 hour) and transcript retention — write straight to ~/.claude/settings.json, only on your interaction, so you can change the cache TTL without leaving Pits.
  • Row layout refresh. A Finder-style disclosure chevron in the gutter (the whole left edge toggles the row), the status/working indicator moved up beside the project label, and the filter controls relocated to the leading edge next to the month picker.
  • Testing + cleanup foundation. The release’s original scope: an extract-and-snapshot testing convention (derived view state lifted into pure static func helpers that tests assert against), the Thread.sleep retry removed from OpenSessionsWatcher’s main-actor path, a VoiceOver label on the filter toggle, and HumanTurn/SessionTitle relocated into Pits/Models/.
  • Under the hood: cache schema → v9, so the first launch re-parses your history from the JSONL transcripts once — rebuilding turn counts and per-turn costs cleanly; 447 tests on macos-26.
